title-group.article-title: Real-world effectiveness of trastuzumab deruxtecan in HER2-low metastatic breast cancer.

contrib-group.aff: Riverside University Medical Center, Chicago, IL
Central Oncology Research Hospital, Houston, TX
Westlake Comprehensive Cancer Center, Seattle, WA

abstract.p: Background: The effectiveness of trastuzumab deruxtecan outside clinical trials remains incompletely characterized for HER2-low metastatic breast cancer. We evaluated treatment patterns, clinical outcomes, and safety in a multi-institutional real-world cohort. Methods: We retrospectively identified consecutive adults with HER2-low metastatic breast cancer who initiated trastuzumab deruxtecan between 2021 and 2025 across six oncology centers. Demographic, clinicopathologic, treatment, and outcome data were abstracted from electronic records using a common data model. The primary endpoint was real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS); secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), overall survival (OS), treatment duration, and grade 3 or higher adverse events. Time-to-event outcomes were estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods. Results: The analysis included 286 patients with a median age of 61 years; 98% were female and the median number of prior systemic treatment lines was two. After a median follow-up of 18.4 months, ORR was 47.2%, median rwPFS was 8.7 months, and median OS was 21.3 months. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events occurred in 24.1% of patients. Interstitial lung disease was documented in 7.0%. In exploratory subgroup analysis, patients with IHC 2+/ISH-negative disease had a median rwPFS of 10.2 months. Conclusions: In routine practice, trastuzumab deruxtecan demonstrated clinically meaningful activity in HER2-low metastatic breast cancer, with outcomes generally consistent with its established treatment role. Toxicity remained manageable, although monitoring for interstitial lung disease is warranted. These findings support continued real-world evaluation in broader and underrepresented patient populations. Research Sponsor: None.
